_meta.source: docs/rian-research-chatgpt.md — annual-average electrical demand planning bands
_meta.caveat: Planning bands, not guaranteed averages; final sizing requires at least one year of hourly site-load data.
_meta.citations: Per-load sources added 2026-08-21 from a verified research pass (data/research/demand-citations.json): 23 bands supported, 18 partially supported, 2 contradicted and corrected in place (offshore platforms, land-based aquaculture), 12 with no authoritative source found. Uncited bands are listed in _meta.uncited and marked on the page.
uncited: Dedicated baseload and outage-protection blocks within larger data-center campuses
Integrated agricultural campuses combining growing, processing, refrigeration and water pumping
Large integrated sawmills and wood-products plants
Large pozzolan mines with onsite crushing, grinding or drying
Remote oil fields and production hubs

loads.label: Regional data centers

sources.label: JLL — Why smaller data centers are taking off
sources.quote: have a smaller capacity between 500 kilowatts to 2 MW

sources.label: Grand View Research — Edge Data Center Market Report
sources.quote: the below 10 MW segment is projected to hold 80.82% of the U.S. edge data center market share in 2026

loads.published: JLL puts edge data centers at 0.5–2 MW; market-report aggregation puts 'metro edge' at 1–5 MW and 'regional edge' at 5–20 MW, with facilities under 10 MW holding ~81% of the projected 2026 U.S. edge-DC market.
loads.delta_note: JLL's edge figure (0.5–2 MW) sits below our 1–10 MW floor; the market-share stat supports the ceiling but is a market-segment share, not a per-facility figure.

loads.label: Company-owned data centers
loads.not_found_note: No authoritative source found breaking out 'company-owned/enterprise' data centers as a distinct MW-sized category. LBNL's 2024 report classifies energy use by space-type share (internal/enterprise vs. colocation vs. hyperscale) rather than per-facility MW.

loads.label: Shared data centers

sources.label: Equinix Interconnections blog — Inside Equinix Data Centers (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figures via search)
sources.quote: Dallas campus has 228,681 sq ft of colocation rental space and 40 MW of sellable power capacity

loads.published: Equinix multi-building metro campuses report 40–113 MW of 'sellable power capacity' per metro (Dallas campus: 40 MW across 228,681 sq ft; DC-metro: 113 MW across 13 interconnected buildings).
loads.delta_note: These are 2019-dated metro-wide totals across multiple buildings, not single shared-facility figures; the upper end (113 MW) exceeds our 50 MW ceiling.

loads.label: Supercomputing centers

sources.label: Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (ORNL) — Powering Frontier
sources.quote: We needed to provide about 40 megawatts of power and cooling to the Frontier data center.

loads.published: ORNL provisioned ~40 MW of power and cooling for the Frontier exascale supercomputer (operating draw ~21–23 MW); peer exascale machines El Capitan (~30 MW, LLNL) and Aurora (~38.7 MW, Argonne) fall in the same range.

loads.label: AI and very large cloud data centers
loads.note: total, using a 1–20 MW dedicated block
loads.band_full: 50–500+ MW total, using a 1–20 MW dedicated block

sources.label: Congressional Research Service R48646, Data Centers and Their Energy Consumption (via EveryCRSReport mirror)
sources.quote: new hyperscale data centers have been built with capacities from 100 MW to 1,000 MW each

sources.label: JLL — Why smaller data centers are taking off
sources.quote: can typically house 10,000 racks with a capacity in excess of 80 megawatts

loads.published: CRS: a facility must exceed 100 MW power rating to count as 'hyperscale'; new hyperscale data centers are built at 100–1,000 MW each. JLL: hyperscale halls exceed 80 MW with 10,000+ racks.
loads.delta_note: Published hyperscale floor (100 MW, CRS) is double our band's 50 MW floor; our 500+ MW ceiling matches the observed 1,000 MW top end. No source addresses the '1–20 MW dedicated block' sub-claim; phased-buildout trade press describes larger 24–72 MW installment blocks.

loads.label: Dedicated baseload and outage-protection blocks within larger data-center campuses
loads.delta_note: This describes total campus grid-interconnection phasing, a different concept from a microreactor-sized backup block, with larger increments than our 1–20 MW band.
loads.not_found_note: No source found addressing microreactor-scale 'dedicated baseload/outage-protection block' sizing within data-center campuses specifically. Related but distinct: trade press on phased hyperscale buildouts cites 24–72 MW power-delivery increments per construction phase. Context source (does not support the band): https://build.inc/insights/data-center-campus-development-site-criteria

loads.label: Large pozzolan mines with onsite crushing, grinding or drying
loads.not_found_note: No source found with pozzolan-specific MW figures after two search angles. General mining-industry context only: comminution (crushing+grinding) accounts for ~53% of total mine energy use industry-wide, and natural pozzolan needs only minimal processing (crush to <5mm, dry) versus a full metal-ore comminution circuit — consistent with pozzolan mines sitting at the small end of the mining spectrum, but no independent MW figure was found to confirm the 1–5 MW band itself.

loads.label: Remote lithium and rare-earth mines with onsite processing

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: Of the mines referenced in the UAA (2020) study, electric power capacity ranges from 10 to 40 MW.

sources.label: OPG/CNL/MIRARCO — SMR Economic Feasibility and Cost-Benefit Study for Remote Mining
sources.quote: increase to a maximum of 210,818 MW·he in year 9, then decrease to 167,079 MW·he at the end of the LoM

loads.published: No lithium/rare-earth-specific figure found; general remote-mine data points run at or slightly above this band's ceiling. INL/GAIN (citing UAA 2020, Alaska mines): electric power capacity 10–40 MW. OPG/CNL/MIRARCO representative Arctic mine: annual electricity consumption implies ~19–24 MW average over its 14-year life.
loads.delta_note: Both figures are for unspecified/base-metal remote mines, not lithium or rare-earth specifically (which involve heavier chemical processing and could plausibly run higher); both land at or above our 20 MW ceiling rather than inside the 5–20 MW band.

loads.label: Remote copper and other large mines
loads.note: for a representative site, with larger mines using a 5–20 MW partial-power block
loads.band_full: 12–25 MW for a representative site, with larger mines using a 5–20 MW partial-power block

sources.label: OPG/CNL/MIRARCO — SMR Economic Feasibility and Cost-Benefit Study for Remote Mining
sources.quote: increase to a maximum of 210,818 MW·he in year 9, then decrease to 167,079 MW·he at the end of the LoM

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: electric power capacity ranges from 10 to 40 MW

sources.label: Reuters Events Nuclear — Ontario Power Generation predicts SMR openings in booming mining sectors
sources.quote: A typical mine might require around 30 MW of power capacity, while a smelter might require as much as 200 MW of power

loads.published: OPG/CNL/MIRARCO's representative far-North Canadian mine (real anonymized mining-company data, unspecified commodity): annual electricity consumption peaks at 210,818 MWh in year 9 (~24 MW average) and settles at 167,079 MWh (~19 MW average) by end of mine life — squarely inside the 12–25 MW band. INL/GAIN corroborates with a 10–40 MW range across UAA-surveyed Alaska mines. Reuters Events, reporting on this same OPG-adjacent research: 'a typical mine might require around 30 MW.'
loads.delta_note: Reuters' 'typical mine ~30 MW' figure sits just above our 25 MW ceiling; a downstream smelter (200 MW) is an order of magnitude larger and is correctly excluded from this band.

loads.label: Individual remote grids with sufficient year-round demand

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: These isolated micro- and mini- grids range in size from 0.5–85 MWe, serving both communities and industry

loads.published: INL/GAIN, citing UAA (2020a): Alaska's isolated micro/mini-grids (over 100 communities) range 0.5–85 MWe; the report frames near-term (2020s) microreactor deployment as targeting isolated microgrids of 100 kWe–20 MWe.
loads.delta_note: The 0.5–85 MW published range is much wider than our 1–10 MW band; our band sits at the lower/typical end of that spread rather than being independently pinned down.

loads.label: Regional grids serving several communities

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: Puerto Rico's Integrated Resource Plan proposes building a new electricity infrastructure with microgrids (1–20 MW)

loads.published: INL/GAIN: Puerto Rico's Integrated Resource Plan proposes new resilience-focused electricity infrastructure built as 1–20 MW microgrids; IRENA (cited in the same report) puts renewable mini-grid capacity generally from kW up to 100+ MW.

loads.label: Replacements or partial replacements for older diesel and coal generation

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: plant unit sizes ranging from 100 MW to 1,000 MW, with most U.S. coal plants in the mid-range of 250–750 MWe

loads.published: INL/GAIN: U.S. coal-plant unit sizes typically run 100–1,000 MW (most in the 250–750 MWe mid-range) — far above this band at whole-plant scale. Diesel-side context (Puerto Rico, Alaska microgrids) matches the 1–20 MW band well.
loads.delta_note: A 1–20 MW microreactor cannot replace a full 100–1,000 MW coal unit; the band's own wording ('partial replacements') already anticipates this and is best read as a fractional offset, not a like-for-like swap. It fits diesel-generator-scale replacement much better than utility coal-plant-scale replacement.

loads.label: Power for new mines, factories, data centers and communities before major grid upgrades

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: markets subject to fuel insecurity and high-energy prices (mining, islands) and on isolated microgrids (100 kWe–20 MWe)

loads.published: Same Puerto Rico IRP data point applies: new resilience/bridge electricity infrastructure proposed as 1–20 MW microgrids, and the INL/GAIN 2020s-deployment window frames microreactors as fitting isolated microgrids of 100 kWe–20 MWe before later (2030s) integration into 1–100 MWe mini-grids.

loads.label: Staged additions for future load growth

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: Later in the 2030s, microreactors begin to be integrated into mini-grids (1 MWe to 100 MWe)

loads.published: INL/GAIN frames a two-stage timeline: 2020s deployment onto isolated microgrids (100 kWe–20 MWe), then 'later in the 2030s, microreactors begin to be integrated into mini-grids (1 MWe to 100 MWe)' — i.e. staged growth is described, but the report's own second stage already exceeds our 20 MW ceiling.
loads.delta_note: The band matches INL's first (2020s) stage but not its own second (2030s) stage, which runs up to 100 MWe — 'staged additions' as a concept is supported, but the ceiling stated (20 MW) is lower than where INL sees the staging heading.

loads.label: Steel rolling and finishing plants, excluding full steelmaking mills

sources.label: ScienceDirect — Energy and environmental performance of iron and steel industry in real-time demand response: a case of hot rolling process (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figure via search)
sources.quote: demand response potential peaks at 16 MW ... in a hot rolling process with 5 roughing mills and 7 finishing mills

loads.published: A hot-rolling-process case study (5 roughing mills + 7 finishing mills, no EAF) reports demand-response peaking at 16 MW — inside the band. Primary steelmaking (electric arc furnace), explicitly excluded by our label, peaks far higher at 100+ MW.

loads.label: Cement plants

sources.label: Energy Science & Engineering (Wiley) — power generation from cement kiln waste gases, Kenya case study (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figure via search)
sources.quote: average electricity demand of 9.7 MW (peak)

loads.published: A peer-reviewed Kenyan cement-plant case study reports average electricity demand of 9.7 MW (peak) — inside the band. An LBNL/DOE report on California cement plants (fetched) discusses demand-response strategy but does not itself state plant-level MW figures.

loads.label: Lime plants
loads.not_found_note: No plant-level MW figure found. Only a specific-energy figure surfaced (~20 kWh electricity per tonne of lime), which would require an unstated production-rate assumption to convert to MW — not converted here to avoid presenting a derived number as a published one.

loads.label: Chemical plants
loads.note: with a 5–20 MW block at larger plants
loads.band_full: 5–50 MW, with a 5–20 MW block at larger plants

sources.label: INL/GAIN — Global Market Analysis of Microreactors (INL/EXT-21-63214)
sources.quote: most applicable to chemical, paper and food manufacturing particularly in the range of 10 to 50 MWth

sources.label: Thunder Said Energy — Industrial energy and electricity consumption by sector (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: as high as 10MW at typical auto plants and 25MW at typical steel mills

loads.published: No chemical-specific electrical MW figure isolated; a general industrial-energy source cites 'as high as 10 MW at typical auto plants and 25 MW at typical steel mills' without a distinct chemical-plant number. INL/GAIN, citing Forsberg and Foss (2021), places chemical/paper/food process-heat demand mostly in the 10–50 MWth range, with >6,000 U.S. heat users above 1 MWth.
loads.delta_note: The INL/Forsberg-Foss figure is THERMAL demand (MWth, process steam/heat), not electrical — a different metric than our electrical-demand band, though similar in magnitude at the low end.

loads.label: Fertilizer plants
loads.note: with a 5–20 MW block at larger plants
loads.band_full: 5–30 MW, with a 5–20 MW block at larger plants

sources.label: MDPI Fuels — Flexible Green Ammonia Production Plants (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figure via search)
sources.quote: a typically sized Haber-Bosch plant with an air separation unit will require between 28 and 44 MW of 24/7 electricity supply

loads.published: A typically sized Haber-Bosch ammonia plant with an air separation unit requires 28–44 MW of round-the-clock electricity — just above our band's ceiling, consistent with the dataset's own 'block at larger plants' framing.
loads.delta_note: 28–44 MW sits just above our 30 MW whole-plant ceiling but matches the '5–20 MW block at larger plants' framing well if read as a partial supply.

loads.label: Hydrogen and low-carbon fuel plants

sources.label: Search synthesis of green-ammonia/electrolyzer trade coverage (not independently fetched)
sources.quote: Small-scale ammonia plants can be powered by alkaline electrolyzer units with capacities of 1 MW, 5 MW, and 10 MW

loads.published: Small-scale green-ammonia/hydrogen electrolyzer units are sold in 1 MW, 5 MW and 10 MW module sizes, consistent with a 5–20 MW production block. Fertiglobe's Egypt phase-one green-hydrogen plant is a 100 MW electrolyzer array (whole-facility scale, feeding ammonia production).
loads.delta_note: Individual electrolyzer modules (1–10 MW) support the band; whole-facility hydrogen plants (e.g. Fertiglobe's 100 MW Egypt array) are much larger once multiple blocks are combined.

loads.label: Pulp and paper mills
loads.band_full: 10–40 MW, with partial supply above 20 MW

sources.label: ScienceDirect — The chemical pulp mill as a flexible prosumer of electricity (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figures via search)
sources.quote: momentary net production ranges from 17 MW in the least-flexible scenario to 105 MW in the most-flexible scenario

loads.published: A 1,000-tonne/day Kraft mill can generate 25–35 MW from black-liquor combustion alone — inside the band. A chemical-pulp-mill flexibility study reports net electricity production spanning 17–105 MW across operating scenarios.
loads.delta_note: The flexibility study's upper end (105 MW) is well above our 40 MW ceiling; the core Kraft self-generation figure (25–35 MW) fits inside the band.

loads.label: Large integrated sawmills and wood-products plants
loads.not_found_note: No per-mill MW figure found. USDA Forest Service and Oregon Dept. of Forestry sources report only aggregate/industry-wide energy (trillion-Btu scale across dozens of mills) and per-unit-of-lumber intensity, not per-facility electrical demand — converting would require assumptions the sources don't state.

loads.label: Semiconductor fabs
loads.note: total, using a 5–20 MW dedicated block
loads.band_full: 30–150+ MW total, using a 5–20 MW dedicated block

sources.label: SemiWiki — Power consumption of fabs through the roof, danger ahead?
sources.quote: a typical semiconductor manufacturing plant consumes as much energy annually as about 50,000 homes

sources.label: PatentPC — Semiconductor Manufacturing Energy Consumption (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: Leading-edge fabs require 200–600 MW of reliable, clean power

loads.published: SemiWiki, citing McKinsey: a typical semiconductor fab consumes as much energy annually as ~50,000 homes (implies roughly 60 MW average). Other trade reporting cites leading-edge fabs requiring 200–600 MW.
loads.delta_note: Leading-edge fabs (200–600 MW per trade estimates) run above our 150 MW open ceiling; a 'typical' fab (~60 MW implied) fits inside the band.

loads.label: Battery-cell plants
loads.band_full: 20–100+ MW total, using a 5–20 MW block

sources.label: IOP Science — Energy use for GWh-scale lithium-ion battery production
sources.quote: The average power demand correlating to an annual electricity consumption of 2300 GWh is over 250 MW

loads.published: Peer-reviewed (IOP Science topical review): Tesla Gigafactory Nevada's ~2,300 GWh/year electricity use implies an average power demand 'over 250 MW'; Northvolt Ett's first 8 GWh/year production line implies ~46 MW average — both anchor within or near the band's open-ended range.
loads.delta_note: Gigafactory Nevada is a multi-product gigafactory (cells plus drivetrain components), not a single battery-cell line, which likely inflates its total above a pure-play battery-cell plant; the single-line Northvolt figure (46 MW) fits the band more directly.

loads.label: Battery-material plants
loads.not_found_note: No plant-level MW figure found after two search angles covering cathode/material producers generally and named companies (Redwood Materials, Li-Cycle, Ascend Elements) specifically.

loads.label: Battery-recycling plants
loads.not_found_note: No plant-level MW figure found. Tangential: Redwood Materials operates a 12 MW/63 MWh battery microgrid at its Nevada site, but it powers a co-located third-party AI data center, not the recycling/materials plant itself, so it is not used as a proxy here.

loads.label: Remote oil fields and production hubs
loads.not_found_note: No figure specific to a single remote onshore oil-field production hub was found with confidence after two search angles. Nearby but not equivalent: FPSOs (floating offshore production) typically run 80–150 MW, and one source's claim of '500 MW for remote drilling operations' could not be confirmed as a per-site figure, so it is not used.

loads.label: Offshore platforms
loads.note: total; documented platforms, FPSOs and North Sea hubs, using a 5–20 MW partial-power block
loads.band_full: 80–300+ MW total; documented platforms, FPSOs and North Sea hubs, using a 5–20 MW partial-power block

sources.label: MDPI Energies — Electrification of Offshore Oil and Gas Production (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figures via search)
sources.quote: The power demand of a single platform can easily exceed 100 megawatts (MW)

sources.label: SIA Partners — Offshore Oil and Gas Platforms: Electrification Technologies (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: Hywind Tampen will have a total capacity of 60 MW and will provide approximately 35% of the electricity demand of the Gullfaks and Snorre oil and gas fields

loads.published: Published figures run well above this band: a single offshore platform's power demand 'can easily exceed 100 MW,' with complex deepwater systems needing 100–250 MW depending on subsea loads; FPSOs typically 80–150 MW; Norway's Johan Sverdrup phase 2 expanded power-from-shore capacity to 300 MW total, and the 60 MW Hywind Tampen floating wind array covers only ~35% of the combined Gullfaks/Snorre fields' demand.
loads.delta_note: Corrected 2026-08-21: this dataset previously claimed 10–50 MW total. Published figures run 2–10× higher (single platforms exceed 100 MW; FPSOs 80–150 MW; Johan Sverdrup shore power 300 MW), so the band now follows the sources. Real single-platform and platform-hub demand runs 2–10x above our 10–50 MW band. The band may be intended as a microreactor-sized partial contribution ('5–20 MW block') rather than whole-platform demand, but even that reading is generous against these figures — a genuinely small/older single platform could still fit this band, but the well-documented examples found here (North Sea hubs, FPSOs) do not.

loads.label: Pipeline pumping and electric compression stations

sources.label: INGAA — Assessment of Electric-Drive Compressor Conversion (Jan 2024)
sources.quote: The average per-station estimated load is 11 MW ... more than 80% of compressor stations are rated under 21 MW

loads.published: INGAA (Interstate Natural Gas Association of America), surveying 1,395 U.S. compressor stations: peak load ranges <1–97 MW, average per-station load is 11 MW, over 50% are rated under 8 MW, and over 80% are rated under 21 MW — closely matching this band.

loads.label: Gas-processing plants
loads.not_found_note: No gas-processing-plant-specific MW figure was isolated separately from LNG liquefaction and pipeline-compression data (which are covered in adjacent rows).

loads.label: Smaller liquefied-natural-gas plants and receiving terminals

sources.label: ScienceDirect — Flexible operation of a mixed fluid cascade LNG plant for electrical power management (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figure via search)
sources.quote: operating range from 3.5 MW to 28 MW

sources.label: LNG Industry — Ensuring stable power (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: For a 5 million tpy liquefaction facility, roughly 140 MW of power supply is needed

loads.published: A flexible-operation LNG plant study demonstrates a power range of 3.5–28 MW; a mini-scale LNG unit (~35 kton/yr) draws ~3.5 MW. By contrast, large liquefaction trains (5–18 million tpy) need 140–800 MW — the 'large' facilities this dataset explicitly excludes.

loads.label: Smaller refineries

sources.label: Schneider Electric blog — How process electrification can decarbonize oil refineries and petrochemicals (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: a typical medium-complexity refinery requires around 700-900 MW of thermal power and over 50 MW of electricity

loads.published: A medium-complexity refinery reportedly needs 'over 50 MW' of electricity (alongside 700–900 MW of thermal energy); a separate estimate puts a refinery's 'useful' electrical draw at ~24 MW. Electricity is generally only ~5–10% of a refinery's total energy use.
loads.delta_note: Even a 'medium-complexity' (not just large) refinery appears to need somewhat more than our 20 MW ceiling on one estimate (>50 MW); the second estimate (~24 MW) sits right at the ceiling.

loads.label: Dedicated electrical blocks at larger refineries

sources.label: Schneider Electric blog — How process electrification can decarbonize oil refineries and petrochemicals (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: a typical medium-complexity refinery requires around 700-900 MW of thermal power and over 50 MW of electricity

loads.published: Same refinery data applies: if a whole medium-complexity refinery draws roughly 50+ MW of electricity, a 5–20 MW 'dedicated block' is a plausible partial slice of that total, consistent with the band's own 'block' framing, though no source directly names a block size.

loads.label: Large Amazon, Walmart and similar fulfillment and distribution centers
loads.note: normally; 2–10 MW with heavy automation or fleet charging
loads.band_full: 1–3 MW normally; 2–10 MW with heavy automation or fleet charging

sources.label: NREL/OpenEI — Heavy-Duty Electric Fleet Depot Charging Load Profiles & Substation Load Integration Assessment (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: A 20-bus transit depot charging overnight at 150 kW per bus could draw 3 MW of peak demand

loads.published: No fulfillment-center-specific published figure found directly. Heavy-duty fleet-depot charging (the 'fleet charging' half of this claim) draws roughly 3 MW peak for a 20-vehicle bus depot and ~4.5 MW for a 50-bus depot, consistent with the 2–10 MW automated/fleet-charging upper case.

loads.label: Refrigerated distribution centers

sources.label: Ally Energy — Logistics Facility Electrification, Load Growth, and Demand Side Control
sources.quote: A cold storage warehouse can consume 1 to 3 megawatts

loads.published: A cold storage warehouse can consume 1 to 3 megawatts — inside the band.

loads.label: Cargo-port electrical systems combining terminal operations and ship plug-in power
loads.band_full: 5–20 MW average, with higher short-term peaks

sources.label: ICCT — Shore power needs and CO2 implications working paper (fetch blocked, HTTP 403; figures via search)
sources.quote: a large cruise ship may require a constant supply of up to 16 MW, while a container ship may require 7.5 MW

loads.published: Per-vessel and per-crane figures, not a whole-port average: a large cruise ship's shore-power connection needs up to 16 MW, a container ship ~7.5 MW (6–12 MVA typical container-ship connections, 10–16 MVA for cruise ships); ship-to-shore cranes draw 1–2 MW each when operating. A terminal serving several berths and cranes concurrently would plausibly aggregate into the 5–20 MW band, though no single published 'whole cargo port' figure was found.

loads.label: Major passenger airports

sources.label: Port of Seattle — 2024 CO2 Emissions from Scope 1 & 2 Sources at SEA Airport
sources.quote: TOTAL ELECTRICITY ... 122,530,683 [kWh, 2024 column]

loads.published: Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) purchased 122,530,683 kWh of total electricity in 2024 per the Port of Seattle's own emissions inventory — equivalent to an average continuous demand of ~14 MW (122,530,683 kWh ÷ 8,760 h), inside the 10–30 MW band. Figure is a direct unit-conversion of the report's own annual total, not independently stated as MW by the source.

loads.label: Major air-cargo campuses
loads.not_found_note: No directly stated air-cargo-campus MW figure found after two search angles. FedEx's $1.5B Memphis World Hub expansion required a new dedicated substation (capacity undisclosed in press coverage); FedEx Ground's Pittsburgh campus has a ~4 MW solar carport reported to offset roughly 30% of campus power, but converting that to a demand figure would require assumptions (solar capacity factor, energy vs. peak basis) the source doesn't supply.

loads.label: Large rail, truck and fleet-charging hubs
loads.band_full: 1–10 MW average, with peaks of 5–30 MW

sources.label: NREL/OpenEI — Heavy-Duty Electric Fleet Depot Charging Load Profiles & Substation Load Integration Assessment (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: A 20-bus transit depot charging overnight at 150 kW per bus could draw 3 MW of peak demand

loads.published: Heavy-duty fleet depot charging: a 20-bus depot at 150 kW/bus overnight draws ~3 MW peak; a 50-bus depot at 90 kW average/bus needs ~4.5 MW peak electrical service; the new Megawatt Charging System (MCS) standard supports up to 3.75 MW per individual charging point. ICCT projects county-level aggregate medium/heavy-duty-vehicle charging could reach 132 MW by 2030 in high-energy industrial counties — an aggregate across many sites, not one hub.
loads.delta_note: Individual depot peaks found (3–4.5 MW) sit at the low end of our 1–10 MW average band and well under our 30 MW peak ceiling; no source confirms a hub actually reaching the 30 MW peak this band allows for.

loads.label: Large individual hospitals

sources.label: DOE Better Buildings — Combined Heat and Power (CHP) Market Sector Fact Sheet: Hospitals
sources.quote: The current average CHP installation size at a U.S. hospital is ~3.3 MW.

loads.published: DOE Better Buildings CHP fact sheet: the average CHP installation size at a U.S. hospital is ~3.3 MW — inside the band. A named small-hospital example (Doctors Community Hospital, Lanham, MD) uses 1.2 MW of CHP to cover 80% of its electrical load, implying ~1.5 MW total demand.

loads.label: Major medical campuses

sources.label: DOE Better Buildings — Combined Heat and Power (CHP) Market Sector Fact Sheet: Hospitals
sources.quote: the campus installed 15 MW of CHP capacity to provide electricity, hot water, steam, and cooling

loads.published: Same DOE fact sheet, named multi-hospital campus examples: UF Health Shands Healthcare Campus (Gainesville, FL — multiple teaching hospitals, research facilities, trauma center) installed 4.3 MW of CHP in 2009 plus 7.4 MW more in 2017 (11.7 MW total); University of Texas Medical Branch (Galveston — 7 hospitals, clinics, academic/research buildings, 13,000 employees) installed 15 MW of CHP in 2016. Both fall inside the band.

loads.label: Large prison complexes

sources.label: DOE Better Buildings — Combined Heat and Power (CHP) Market Sector Fact Sheet: Correctional Facilities
sources.quote: The average CHP system at a correctional facility has a capacity of 2.4 MW.

loads.published: DOE Better Buildings CHP fact sheet: 'The average CHP system at a correctional facility has a capacity of 2.4 MW' (44 facilities, 124 MW total installed) — inside the band. Corroborating scale proxies: California's 12 solar-equipped state prisons average ~2.3 MW of solar capacity each; Santa Rita Jail's 1 MW fuel cell covers up to 80% of peak demand (implying ~1.25 MW total).

loads.label: Major universities

sources.label: DOE Better Buildings — Combined Heat and Power (CHP) Market Sector Fact Sheet: Colleges & Universities
sources.quote: The average CHP system at a college/university has a capacity of 9.1 MW.

loads.published: DOE Better Buildings CHP fact sheet: 'The average CHP system at a college/university has a capacity of 9.1 MW' (281 institutions, 2.6 GW total installed) — inside the band. University of Minnesota (Minneapolis) installed a 22.8 MW CHP system, also inside the band near its ceiling.
loads.delta_note: A search-only data point (not independently fetched) put one large university's total purchased electricity at ~400,000 MWh/yr (~46 MW average) — above our 30 MW ceiling — suggesting the largest flagship campuses can exceed this band even though the CHP-fleet average sits comfortably inside it.

loads.delta_note: This is one facility's provisioned power on a national-lab site, not a whole-lab total — used here only as a lower-bound sanity check, not direct confirmation.

loads.published: DOE Better Buildings CHP fact sheet: 227 WWTPs with CHP total 755 MW installed (~3.3 MW average). Named example: Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Department (a major-city utility) runs 12.8 MW of cogeneration capacity across two facilities — both inside the band.

loads.label: Large seawater desalination plants

sources.label: DOE — Bandwidth Study on Energy Use and Potential Energy Savings Opportunities in U.S. Seawater Desalination Systems (2017)
sources.quote: A value of 2.7 kWhe/m3 (with energy recovery) at the Carlsbad facility for the current typical

loads.published: DOE bandwidth study: the Carlsbad, California facility (the single largest U.S. seawater RO plant, 54% of national capacity, sized at 50 MGD / 189,300 m3/day) runs at a current-typical energy intensity of 2.7 kWh(e)/m3 — implying ~21.3 MW average electric demand (189,300 m3/day × 2.7 kWh/m3 ÷ 24h), essentially matching the band's ceiling.
loads.delta_note: ~21.3 MW is a derived figure (source states energy intensity and capacity separately, not a combined MW value) and sits just above our 20 MW ceiling for the single largest U.S. plant — a reasonable calibration point for the band's upper end.

sources.quote: Electricity demand was as low as 1.5 MW in the afternoon but spiked to 11 MW at night to power grow lights

loads.published: DOE Better Buildings CHP fact sheet: greenhouse CHP installations average 3 MW (post-2005, down from >100 MW utility-scale cogeneration plants in the 1990s). Named example: Houweling's Tomatoes (six greenhouses, Camarillo, CA) had electricity demand 'as low as 1.5 MW in the afternoon' spiking to '11 MW at night to power grow lights.'
loads.delta_note: The named campus's night-time lighting peak (11 MW) runs slightly above our 8 MW ceiling; its daytime low (1.5 MW) and the CHP fleet average (3 MW) both fit inside the band.

sources.label: US Patent — Systems and methods of intensive recirculating aquaculture (via search synthesis, not directly fetched)
sources.quote: electrical energy consumption installed estimated at 16,000 kW

loads.published: Two data points bracket our band from opposite sides rather than falling inside it: a patent describing an intensive recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) cites installed electrical capacity of ~16 MW at full scale (above our 5 MW ceiling), while one unspecified 'fishery' consumed 4.1 million kWh/yr (~0.47 MW average, below our 1 MW floor).
loads.delta_note: Corrected 2026-08-21: previously 1–5 MW. The two published data points sit on either side of that band, neither inside it. Land-based RAS (recirculating aquaculture system) facilities are unusually energy-intensive (continuous pumping, aeration, filtration, temperature control), which may explain why a large intensive system runs well above this band; a much smaller operation runs well below it. The 1–5 MW band may be describing a mid-size case this research didn't surface.
